title: Worst Cocktails for Hangovers: 10 Drinks Ranked by Risk
excerpt: Which cocktails cause the worst hangovers and why: hidden alcohol, sugar, bubbles, caffeine, and congeners. A ranked list from punch bowls to vodka sodas, plus gentler swaps.
metaDescription: Which cocktails cause the worst hangovers? 10 drinks ranked by risk, why sugar, bubbles and caffeine make it worse, and gentler cocktails to order instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the worst cocktails for a hangover aren't the ones with some secret toxic ingredient. They're the ones that get more alcohol into you than you meant to drink. Big multi-spirit drinks like the Long Island iced tea, party punches of unknown strength, and sweet frozen drinks go down like juice while delivering two or three drinks' worth of alcohol each. Energy-drink cocktails keep you feeling awake long after your body has had enough. Dark-spirit cocktails add a second factor, congeners, which controlled studies link to worse hangovers. Below is a ranking from worst to gentlest, with the reasons behind each, and a short list of cocktails that are easier on you the next day.

**The quick rules:** Count each cocktail by the alcohol in it, not as "one drink." Be wary of anything that tastes mostly like sugar or fruit, anything served in a pitcher or a bowl, and anything mixed with an energy drink. Sip fizzy drinks slowly. Pick clear spirits with soda water when you want something lighter, alternate every cocktail with a glass of water, eat a proper meal, and stop a couple of hours before bed.

> **When to see a doctor.** A rough morning after a night of cocktails is common and passes on its own, usually within a day. Get medical help **right away** (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake or can't be woken, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and sweet or strong cocktails make it easier to get there without noticing. Also see a doctor if you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, have severe stomach pain, can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, or if your "hangover" symptoms are still bad after 24 hours. If you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious every time you stop drinking, that is worth raising with a doctor too, plainly and without embarrassment.

## Why Cocktails Give You a Worse Hangover

A hangover is mostly a dose problem. The more alcohol you take in, and the faster you take it in, the worse the next morning tends to be. Cocktails tend to push both of those numbers up, through a handful of mechanisms that stack on top of each other.

### 1. A cocktail is rarely "one drink"

In the US, a standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's the amount in 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof spirits. Many classic cocktails contain more than one shot of spirits, and some add a liqueur on top. A margarita made with 2 ounces of tequila and an ounce of orange liqueur is closer to two standard drinks than one. A Long Island iced tea, which combines vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and orange liqueur, can land somewhere around two to three standard drinks depending on how heavy the pours are. Bars vary a lot, and a "double" or a large glass can push any cocktail higher.

If you think you had four drinks and you actually had seven or eight standard drinks, the hangover will match the real number, not the one in your head.

### 2. Sweet and sour mixers hide the alcohol

Sugar, citrus, cream, and fruit purée all mask the burn of alcohol. That's the point of many cocktails, and it's also the problem. When a drink tastes like lemonade, you drink it like lemonade: faster and in bigger sips. That pace matters, because your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many people, and anything faster than that piles up in your blood.

It's worth being clear about what sugar does and doesn't do. **There is no good evidence that sugar on its own causes hangovers.** Its effect is mostly indirect, through how fast and how much you drink. We go into more detail in our guide to [sugar and hangovers](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover).

### 3. Diet mixers can raise your blood alcohol

This one surprises people. Swapping a regular mixer for a diet one seems like the healthier choice, but a study by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that vodka mixed with a diet soda produced higher breath alcohol levels than the same amount of vodka mixed with a regular sugared soda. The likely reason is that sugar slows the rate the stomach empties into the small intestine, where most alcohol is absorbed. Without the sugar, the alcohol reaches your bloodstream faster. A diet mixer doesn't make a drink worse in every way, but it doesn't make it gentler either.

### 4. Bubbles can speed up absorption

Carbonated drinks seem to move through the stomach faster, which can raise blood alcohol more quickly. Research on champagne and on spirits mixed with carbonated water has pointed in this direction, though people respond differently and not every study found a big effect. In practice, this means a highball or a sparkling cocktail can hit faster than its size suggests, especially on an empty stomach. Our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers the bubbles question in more depth.

### 5. Congeners in dark spirits

Congeners are the by-products of fermentation and aging that give dark spirits their color and flavor. They include small amounts of methanol, other alcohols, and various aldehydes and esters. A well-known controlled study led by Damaris Rohsenow, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, gave people bourbon or vodka to the same breath alcohol level and found that bourbon produced worse hangovers on average. The difference was real but modest, and it was much smaller than the difference between drinking a lot and drinking a little. Cocktails built on whiskey, brandy, or dark rum carry this extra load. For the full picture, see our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### 6. Caffeine and late nights

Energy drinks, espresso, and cola add caffeine. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol, but it can make you feel more alert than you are, which makes it easier to keep ordering. It also cuts into sleep, and poor sleep is one of the biggest reasons people feel terrible the next morning. Our guide to [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) explains what happens when you combine them.

### What about mixing different alcohols?

The old saying "beer before liquor, never sicker" doesn't hold up. A 2019 controlled trial from researchers at Witten/Herdecke University and the University of Cambridge, published in *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, had volunteers drink beer then wine, or wine then beer, and found that the order made no meaningful difference to how bad the hangover was. Total alcohol and how sick people felt while drinking were better predictors. Multi-spirit cocktails feel brutal because they put several shots into one glass, not because the spirits react with each other. More on that in our article on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

## The Worst Cocktails for Hangovers, Ranked

This ranking combines the factors above: how much alcohol a typical serving carries, how well the mixer hides it, how fast people tend to drink it, and whether caffeine, carbonation, or dark-spirit congeners are involved. It's a practical guide, not a lab measurement. A carefully paced old fashioned will treat you better than four "light" drinks downed in an hour.

### 1. Party punch and jungle juice

Punch bowls and jungle juice are at the top for one reason: nobody knows how strong they are, often including the person who made them. These are usually a mix of cheap spirits, sometimes high-proof grain alcohol, poured into fruit juice and soda. The sweetness hides the alcohol completely, the cup gets refilled before it's empty, and it's nearly impossible to count what you've had.

**How to handle it:** If you don't know what's in it, treat each cup as at least two drinks, or skip it and bring something you can measure.

### 2. Long Island iced tea

Despite the name, there's no tea in it. It's vodka, gin, white rum, tequila, and orange liqueur with sour mix and a splash of cola, which gives it an iced-tea color. Depending on the recipe and the bartender, it can carry the alcohol of two to three standard drinks in a single glass, and it tastes far weaker than it is. Order two and you may have had the equivalent of five or six regular drinks.

**How to handle it:** One is plenty. Alternate it with water and don't follow it with a second "round" of anything strong.

### 3. Energy-drink cocktails: vodka Red Bull and Jägerbombs

Mixing alcohol with energy drinks is a recipe for drinking more than you intend. The CDC warns that people who combine the two may feel less drunk than they really are, which can lead them to drink more and take more risks. You still have the same amount of alcohol in your blood. You just stop noticing it as much. The late-night caffeine then wrecks your sleep, and you wake up with a hangover plus the fog and jitters of a short, broken night. Jägerbombs add a sweet herbal liqueur and tend to be drunk as shots, which makes the pace even faster.

We cover the specifics in our guides to [energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol) and the [Jägermeister hangover](/never-hungover/jagermeister-hangover).

### 4. Frozen and blended drinks: margaritas, daiquiris, piña coladas

Frozen drinks are cold enough that you can barely taste the alcohol, and they're often served in large glasses or by the pitcher. A frozen margarita at a chain restaurant can easily hold two shots of tequila plus liqueur, and the slushy texture makes it easy to finish fast. Piña coladas add cream of coconut, which makes them heavy, but the main issue is still the hidden alcohol. Frozen drinks also tend to come with long, sunny afternoons outdoors, where heat and sweat add dehydration to the mix.

**How to handle it:** Ask for a regular-sized glass, drink water between rounds, and be especially careful in the sun. Our page on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains what's really going on with fluid loss.

### 5. Espresso martini

The espresso martini combines vodka, coffee liqueur, and fresh espresso. A typical one carries roughly one and a half standard drinks, plus caffeine late in the evening. That combination makes it easy to keep going and hard to sleep well afterward. If you've ever felt wired and wrecked at the same time the next morning, this drink is a likely suspect. Our full [espresso martini hangover](/never-hungover/espresso-martini-hangover) guide goes through the details.

### 6. Sangria

Sangria is wine mixed with fruit, juice, sugar, and often a splash of brandy or orange liqueur. It tastes mild, gets served by the pitcher, and the fruit soaking in it makes it feel almost wholesome. In reality you're drinking fortified wine that's sweetened to hide its strength. People who get headaches from red wine may also find the base wine itself is part of the problem. See our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) for why that happens.

### 7. Dark-spirit cocktails: old fashioned, Manhattan, dark and stormy, rum punch

These aren't sweet traps in the same way as punch or frozen drinks. An old fashioned or Manhattan is stirred, strong, and usually sipped slowly, which is a point in its favor. The issue is what's in the glass: whiskey, brandy, and dark rum are higher in congeners than vodka or gin. Manhattans and other "up" drinks also tend to contain 2 ounces or more of spirits plus vermouth, so each one is more than a single drink. Rum punch and dark and stormy combine the congener load with sweet mixers or ginger beer, which is where things go wrong fastest.

If dark spirits are your drink, our guides to the [whiskey hangover](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and the [rum hangover](/never-hungover/rum-hangover) explain what to expect.

### 8. Sparkling cocktails: mimosas, French 75s, bellinis

Brunch mimosas feel harmless, and individually they're not very strong. The trouble is the bottomless format, the bubbles that can speed absorption, and the fact that they're usually drunk in the morning or early afternoon, often before a proper meal. A French 75, which adds gin to champagne, is considerably stronger than it tastes.

**How to handle it:** Eat first, set yourself a number before you sit down, and keep a glass of water next to your glass of bubbles.

### 9. Sweet shooters and "candy" shots

Lemon drops, kamikazes, and other sweet shots don't contain a lot of alcohol individually, but they're designed to be drunk in seconds and in rounds. Taking three or four of them in half an hour on top of whatever else you're drinking is a fast way to overshoot. Our guide to [hangover shots](/never-hungover/best-hangover-shots) covers the morning-after kind, which are a different thing entirely.

### 10. Diet-mixer highballs: vodka diet cola and similar

These might look out of place near the bottom of a "worst" list, and that's fair. A single vodka and diet cola is a modest drink. It's here because of the Marczinski and Stamates finding above: without sugar, the alcohol may hit your bloodstream faster, and people often choose diet mixers thinking they're the "lighter" option and then drink more of them. Fine in moderation, but not the safe choice it's often assumed to be.

## Cocktails That Are Gentler on You the Next Day

No cocktail makes a hangover impossible. The total amount of alcohol still matters more than anything else. But some drinks make it much easier to stay in control:

- **Vodka soda, gin and soda, or tequila soda with lime.** One measured pour of a clear spirit, no sugar to hide the alcohol, and a tall glass that takes a while to drink. Vodka and gin are among the lowest-congener spirits. See our [vodka hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and [gin hangover](/never-hungover/gin-hangover) guides for more.
- **A highball with extra soda water.** Ask for a tall glass and a long pour of soda. The drink lasts longer, which naturally slows your pace.
- **Wine spritz.** A small amount of white wine or a light aperitif topped with plenty of soda water stretches one drink across a long glass.
- **Tequila made from 100% agave.** If you like margaritas, ask for one made with 100% agave tequila, fresh lime, and less sweetener, and stick to the regular size. Our [tequila hangover](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) page goes through what the research does and doesn't say about tequila.
- **Single-serve drinks you can count.** A hard seltzer or a measured cocktail you can see being made beats a refilled cup of mystery punch every time.

For a full ranking of drinks from easiest to hardest on the next morning, see [which alcohol gives the least hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## How to Enjoy Cocktails Without Paying for It Tomorrow

You don't have to give up cocktails to avoid feeling terrible. A few habits make a large difference:

1. **Eat a real meal before you start.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Protein, fat, and fiber help most. A handful of bar snacks is better than nothing but not the same.
2. **Count in standard drinks.** If a cocktail has two shots in it, count it as two. Ask the bartender if you're not sure what's in it.
3. **Alternate every cocktail with a glass of water.** It slows your pace and helps you stay hydrated. Water won't cancel out the alcohol, but it helps with thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache.
4. **Pace yourself to about one standard drink an hour.** That's roughly the rate many people's livers clear alcohol, though it varies with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors.
5. **Sip, don't gulp.** This matters most for sweet, frozen, and fizzy drinks, which are the easiest to finish fast.
6. **Skip energy drinks as mixers.** If you want to stay out late, a coffee earlier in the evening is a better idea than caffeine poured into your alcohol.
7. **Stop a couple of hours before bed.** Alcohol close to bedtime fragments sleep, and short sleep makes every hangover worse.
8. **Know your own triggers.** Some people react badly to red wine, dark spirits, or specific liqueurs. If one drink reliably leaves you worse off, believe your own experience.

Our main guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers these habits and the evidence behind them in more depth.

## What to Do If You Already Overdid It

If you're reading this the morning after a cocktail night, here's what tends to help:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water or an oral rehydration drink rather than gulping a large amount at once, especially if you feel queasy. Our page on [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when an electrolyte drink is worth it.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or a simple soup. Your blood sugar may be low, and a bit of food can ease nausea and shakiness.
- **Take an over-the-counter pain reliever carefully, if you need one.** Ibuprofen with food is a common choice for the headache. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking unless a doctor has told you it's fine, because alcohol and acetaminophen together can strain your liver. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Rest.** Sleep is one of the few things that reliably helps, so if you can take it easy for the day, do.
- **Don't drink more to feel better.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover.

Most hangovers ease within a day. If you're getting worse instead of better, or you notice any of the warning signs in the box at the top of this page, get medical help.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Much of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data so far. **There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people,** and it won't change how much alcohol is in a Long Island iced tea. What it can't replace are the basics above: fewer standard drinks, a slower pace, food, water, and sleep.

That said, some people like to add it as one part of their routine on nights they plan to have a few cocktails, and many report that it helps them feel better the next day. If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

The worst cocktails for hangovers are the ones that hide their strength or speed up how fast you drink: punch bowls, Long Island iced teas, energy-drink mixes, and big frozen drinks lead the list. Dark-spirit cocktails add a modest extra hit from congeners, while bubbles and diet mixers can push your blood alcohol up faster. The gentlest options are simple: a clear spirit with soda water, a long highball, or a spritz, drunk slowly, alongside water and food. Count your drinks by what's in them, not by the number of glasses, and the next morning will usually go much better.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Which cocktail gives the worst hangover?**

The drinks most likely to leave you wrecked are the ones that hide how much alcohol you're drinking: party punch or jungle juice, Long Island iced teas, and vodka or Jäger mixed with energy drinks. They aren't chemically special. They simply make it easy to drink three or four standard drinks' worth of alcohol while thinking you've had two. Dark-spirit cocktails come next, because whiskey, brandy, and dark rum carry more congeners, the by-products linked to worse hangovers in controlled studies.

**Why do cocktails give me a worse hangover than beer or wine?**

Usually because you drank more alcohol than you realized. Many cocktails contain one and a half to three standard drinks, sweet and sour mixers hide the taste of the alcohol, and fizzy mixers can speed up absorption. The sugar itself plays a smaller role than its reputation suggests. If you count each cocktail by its actual alcohol content, the difference between cocktails and beer or wine shrinks a lot.

**Does sugar in cocktails cause hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that sugar on its own causes hangovers. Its real effect is indirect: sweetness masks the alcohol, so sugary drinks go down faster and you drink more. Sugar can also make you feel worse if it pushes you to keep drinking or if you skip a real meal. Interestingly, research on mixers found that diet mixers led to higher breath alcohol than sugared ones, so swapping to diet soda does not make a drink safer.

**What is the least hangover-causing cocktail?**

A clear spirit with soda water is the gentlest common option: vodka soda, gin and soda, or tequila soda with lime. One measured pour, no sweet mixer to hide the alcohol, and fewer congeners than dark spirits. A wine spritz topped up with extra soda water is another good pick because it stretches a small amount of wine over a long drink. None of these make a hangover impossible, since the total amount of alcohol still matters most.

**Do mixed drinks with soda get you drunk faster?**

Carbonation appears to speed up how fast alcohol leaves the stomach, so bubbly drinks can raise blood alcohol faster in some people. Studies on champagne and on spirits mixed with carbonated water point in that direction, though not everyone responds the same way. The practical takeaway is to sip fizzy drinks slowly and not treat a highball as a lightweight drink.

**Is a vodka Red Bull worse for a hangover?**

It often is, mainly because of how it makes you drink. The caffeine makes you feel more alert than your blood alcohol level justifies, which the CDC warns can lead people to drink more and take more risks. The late caffeine also damages your sleep, so you wake up tired and foggy on top of the usual hangover. The caffeine does not make you any less drunk.

**Does mixing different alcohols in one cocktail make a hangover worse?**

Mixing types of alcohol is not harmful by itself. A 2019 controlled study that compared beer then wine with wine then beer found that the order made no real difference; the total amount of alcohol did. Multi-spirit drinks like a Long Island iced tea feel worse because they pack several shots into one glass, not because the spirits react with each other.

**Can DHM stop a cocktail hangover?**

There is no good evidence that DHM stops hangovers in people. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, with most of the research coming from animal and lab studies and only limited human data. Some people take it before or after drinking and feel it helps, but it does not change how much alcohol is in your cocktails, and pacing and total drinks matter far more.
